passages.t: Hezekiah's illness, and fifteen years added
passages.happening:
‘In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill’ (verse 1). Isaiah comes to him with the LORD's word: put your house in order, for you are about to die and will not recover.

‘Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD’ (verse 2). He asks the LORD to remember how he has walked before him faithfully and with his whole heart. ‘And Hezekiah wept bitterly’ (verse 3).

The word of the LORD comes to Isaiah again (verse 4). Go and tell Hezekiah: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life’ (verse 5). God will deliver him and the city from the king of Assyria (verse 6). As a sign, the sun's shadow on the stairway of Ahaz will go back ten steps (verses 7-8). ‘So the sunlight went back the ten steps it had descended’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In those days is a loose time marker, and the chapter's place in the book is probably by theme rather than by date. Hezekiah is usually dated to about 715 to 686 BC, so fifteen added years would put the illness around 701 BC, the year of Sennacherib's invasion, which fits the promise of verse 6. The Babylonian embassy of chapter 39 probably came before the 701 campaign as well. On that reading, chapters 38 and 39 step back in time, and the editor placed them after the Assyrian story so that the book can turn toward Babylon.

Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, away from everyone in the room, to pray alone. He weeps. God answers the tears as well as the words.

The stairway of Ahaz was presumably built by Hezekiah's father. Whether it was designed as a sundial or was simply a staircase whose shadow marked the time of day is unknown. The parallel account in 2 Kings 20 tells the same events in a different order.
passages.later: Kings gives the same answer: ‘I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. I will surely heal you’ (2 Kings 20:5). Jeremiah hears the principle behind it: ‘if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring’ (Jeremiah 18:8).
passages.hard:
God announced that Hezekiah would die and then gave him fifteen more years. Did God change his mind?

Read on its surface, the chapter shows God declaring one outcome and then, after prayer, granting another. Christians explain this in more than one way. Many hold that warnings of judgment often carry an unstated condition, as Jeremiah 18 says outright and as the story of Nineveh in Jonah shows: God announces what will happen if nothing changes, precisely so that people will turn to him. On this view his purpose was constant, and the prayer was part of how it came about. Others, who stress God's real relationship with people in time, take the text to mean that God genuinely responds to prayer and changes what he does. Both readings agree that Hezekiah's prayer was heard, and that God's answer was mercy, not a change in his character.

The chapter is not a promise that every prayer for healing will be answered with healing. Many faithful people have prayed and wept and not recovered, and their faith was not lacking.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept, and God answered, ‘I have seen your tears’ (verse 5). Ask whether you have let God see your tears. And ask how you would pray if you were told your time was short.

passages.happening:
‘This is a writing by Hezekiah king of Judah after his illness and recovery’ (verse 9).

He remembers thinking that in the prime of life he must go through the gates of Sheol and never again see the LORD in the land of the living (verses 10-11). His life was being taken down like a shepherd's tent, rolled up like cloth cut from a loom (verse 12). God broke his bones like a lion (verse 13). He chirped like a swallow and moaned like a dove: ‘O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security’ (verse 14).

Then the turn: ‘You have restored me to health and have let me live’ (verse 16). ‘Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back’ (verse 17). Sheol cannot thank God; the dead cannot praise him (verse 18). ‘The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness’ (verse 19). ‘The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Only Isaiah includes this psalm; the account in Kings does not. It has the shape of a psalm of thanksgiving: the danger remembered, the cry for help, the rescue, and the vow to praise.

The pictures of dying are vivid and ordinary. A shepherd's tent was taken down and packed away in a morning. A weaver cut the finished cloth from the loom. Hezekiah felt his life folded up and cut off.

Verse 18 reflects the way much of the Old Testament speaks of death: Sheol is a place of silence, where the dead cannot praise God. That is why recovery means so much to him. He can still give thanks, and fathers can still tell their children of God's faithfulness. Later Scripture, in passages such as Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2, holds out a fuller hope beyond death, but this psalm speaks from inside the older view.
passages.later: The psalms speak the same way of death: ‘For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?’ (Psalm 6:5). And Micah says of God's forgiveness, ‘You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea’ (Micah 7:19).
passages.asks: Hezekiah said that God had cast all his sins behind his back. Ask what you are still carrying that God has already put behind him. And ask what story of God's faithfulness you will tell the next generation.

passages.t: A lump of figs, and a sign
passages.happening:
Isaiah had said to prepare a lump of pressed figs, ‘apply it to the boil, and he will recover’ (verse 21).

And Hezekiah had asked what the sign would be that he would go up to the house of the LORD (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are an afterword. They tell details that the parallel account in 2 Kings 20 gives earlier in the story. The editor added them after the psalm.

A lump of pressed figs applied to a boil was a plain household treatment. Isaiah's instruction joins prayer and medicine. God's promise of healing came through an ordinary treatment. The first hearers would not have seen any conflict between the two.

Hezekiah's question, what sign will show he will go up to the house of the LORD, shows what mattered most to him in his recovery: worship. The sign was the shadow on the stairway.
passages.later: Kings places the figs in the middle of the story: ‘Prepare a poultice of figs’ (2 Kings 20:7). And James tells the church, ‘Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil’ (James 5:14).
passages.asks: Isaiah prescribed a poultice of figs alongside God's promise of healing. Ask whether you treat medicine and prayer as rivals or as partners. And ask whether the first thing you want back after a hard season is the chance to worship.
